title: Thread-safe file tree
idea: A thread-safe file system makes each check-and-change one atomic step, so two threads can never both create one name or see a move half done.

analogy.text: A library with one checkout desk. Many people may browse the shelves at once, but only one person at a time may move books.
analogy.breaks: Browsers here wait while books move; real browsers do not.

points: Checking a name, then adding it, lets a second thread slip in between.
`putIfAbsent` on a concurrent map checks and adds in one atomic call.
A read-write lock lets many readers run together, but a writer runs alone.
Per-directory locks need one global order, or opposite moves can deadlock.

messages.label: containsKey(report.pdf)
messages.note: A checks first. The name is free, so A plans to add it.

messages.label: containsKey(report.pdf)
messages.note: Before A writes, B checks too. It also sees a free name.

messages.label: put(report.pdf, A)
messages.note: A adds its file and reports success to its caller.

messages.label: put(report.pdf, B)
messages.note: B replaces A's file without noticing. Both callers were told created.

messages.label: putIfAbsent(report.pdf)
messages.note: The fix: one atomic call that checks and adds together.

messages.label: null: you won
messages.note: A null result means the name was free and A now owns it.

messages.label: putIfAbsent(report.pdf)
messages.note: B's call runs entirely before or after A's, never in between.

messages.label: existing node
messages.note: B gets A's node back, so the facade throws ALREADY_EXISTS.

code.title: Prove the create race
code.caption: A barrier forces both threads past the check before either writes, so the bug shows on every run. `ConcurrentSkipListMap` is a thread-safe sorted map, like `TreeMap`.

walk.text: Two threads create the same name in the unsafe directory.
The same race against the safe directory; count how many won.
Start both threads, then join them before reading results.
Each step is locked, but the pair is not. Both threads pass the check.
`putIfAbsent` checks and adds as one step, so only one thread wins.

code.title: Read-write lock
code.caption: A two-level model stands in for the tree. Two movers and a reader run at once under one read-write lock. Without the write lock, the reader could see a file in neither folder.

walk.text: Two folders, one file in each; the total size is always 300.
Two threads move files in opposite directions, many thousands of times.
A reader sums sizes and counts any total that is not 300.
A move checks and changes both folders while holding the write lock.
Readers share the read lock, so they never see a file in neither folder.

pitfalls: Never check `containsKey` and then `put` as two steps on shared state.
Hold one lock for the whole move; two separate locks expose a missing file.
If you lock per directory, always take locks in one fixed order.

quiz.q: What is the first line CreateRace prints?
options: It changes from run to run
quiz.why: The barrier makes both threads finish the check before either writes. Both return true, and the second `put` replaces the first, leaving one entry.

takeaway: Check and change in one atomic step; readers share, writers go alone.

starters: When is one tree-wide lock too slow for a file system?
How would per-directory locks with a global order work for move?
Could I use copy-on-write snapshots so readers never wait?
